title: Experiment plan for MethodX (constant fan-in DST)
method: MethodX: sparse-to-sparse dynamic sparse training with a constant fan-in constraint (every active neuron has exactly k incoming weights). Every ΔT steps, per layer: count each neuron's salient weights (layer top-K by weight or by gradient magnitude), ablate neurons with fewer than γ_sal·k salient weights (floor of one) and give their budget to the rest, recompute k′, prune the K smallest-magnitude weights layer-wide, and regrow each active neuron by gradient magnitude up to fan-in k′. ERK (or uniform) layer densities, sparse fan-in-scaled init, update fraction α cosine-decayed to zero at an end fraction, then the mask is frozen. Inference uses a condensed n_active × k values + indices representation with CPU and GPU kernels; a closed-form variance analysis of the output-norm ratio motivates the constraint.

compute.hardware: One to four V100/A100-class GPUs per training run; latency on a Xeon-class workstation CPU and a Volta-generation GPU

claims.text: MethodX learns constant fan-in fine-grained structured sparsity with fully sparse-to-sparse training, and its generalization matches state-of-the-art unstructured DST up to very high sparsity across image-classification architectures
At very high sparsity unstructured DST implicitly ablates whole neurons; a strict constant fan-in constraint prevents this, and dynamic neuron ablation restores unstructured-level accuracy
Neuron ablation can be enabled at all sparsity levels; the resulting width sparsity complements constant fan-in sparsity for real-world inference speed while keeping generalization
The condensed constant fan-in representation is parameter- and memory-efficient and gives real speedups for batch-1 CPU and batched GPU inference versus dense and unstructured sparse representations
Constant fan-in does not impair training dynamics: its output-norm variance is no larger than unstructured sparsity, especially at high sparsity

questions.text: Block A: generalization of MethodX vs unstructured DST, learned N:M and structured baselines across the sparsity grid and architectures
questions.predictionIfFalse: The MethodX − RigL gap grows beyond the pre-registered margin at 95–99% on ImageNet ResNet-50 or ViT
questions.minEffect: Margin to pre-register; example given: within 0.5 pp top-1 of RigL on ImageNet, overlapping 95% CIs on CIFAR

questions.text: Block B: does unstructured DST implicitly ablate neurons at high sparsity, is that linked to the strict constant fan-in accuracy gap, and does it matter causally?
questions.hypothesis: The fraction of ablated neurons in RigL/SET is near 0 at 80% and substantial at 95–99%; full MethodX closes the RigL − strict gap at the same sparsities

questions.text: Block C: does γ_sal act as a width-sparsity knob that trades accuracy against measured latency?
questions.predictionIfFalse: A dense model narrowed to the same per-layer widths and trained from scratch matches (ablation is only finding widths: a weaker story)

questions.text: Block D: is the condensed representation correct, smaller, and faster than dense and the best unstructured implementation on CPU and GPU?
questions.predictionIfFalse: Condensed is slower than dense at moderate sparsity (e.g. ≤ 80%)

questions.text: Block E: do the closed-form output-norm variances match simulation, and does constant fan-in impair signal propagation or training dynamics?
questions.hypothesis: Constant fan-in variance ≤ Bernoulli and exact-count, with the gap widening as sparsity increases

questions.text: Block F: which design choices of MethodX matter (prune scope, saliency, gradient accumulation, layer-wise distribution, sparsified layers, schedule, ablation floor)?
Block F overhead row: what do mask updates cost (wall-clock, training FLOPs incl. the occasional dense gradient, peak memory) vs RigL and SR-STE?

risks.text: Constant fan-in is hardest to satisfy when fan-in is small (1×1 and depthwise convs)
risks.mitigation: include at least one depthwise/compact CNN
